reason: I ranked the scratch transpose and A-panel experiments first because they directly test per-call scratch work or lifetime. B-panel packing and transpose fusion test locality, but add packing or coordination cost. The paired-load proposals have compiler-probe support, but no GEMM timing; they are near-duplicates, so test one representative before spending effort on the repeated variants. Store-path changes have probe support but uncertain full-kernel benefit. The reduction schedule has no measured gain and may complicate numerical validation. Fresh baseline scores vary widely, so none of the historical timing differences establish a cause or a current gain.
